raw_case_text:
We presented a case of a 32-year-old Caucasian male patient with features of immune dysregulation. At the age of 1.5 years, the patient had lymphadenopathy in different lymph node groups, which was initially diagnosed as infection-associated lymphadenitis. At 16 years old, he developed hemolytic anemia, which improved after receiving intravenous immunoglobulin and steroids. After steroid discontinuation, the patient developed pneumonia, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, and thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 38 x 109/L). Bone marrow aspiration results and lymph node biopsy excluded hemoblastosis and indicated reactive lymphadenopathy. The patient's durable lymphopenia and hypogammaglobulinemia raised suspicion of an inborn error of immunity (IEI), and he was referred to immunologists. The target genetic screening for mutations in SN2D1A and BIRC4 genes was negative. The patient was diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency and further treated with a complex therapeutic algorithm including intravenous immunoglobulin replacement, antibiotics, and antifungal drugs. Immunological investigations at diagnosis are demonstrated in  Table 1 . The treatment resulted in partial efficacy in terms of lung foci. In order to treat thrombocytopenia, steroid pulse therapy was administered. As a basic immunosuppressant, azathioprine was started but soon discontinued due to treatment-associated agranulocytosis.
The patient continued to receive steroids, but each attempt to taper the medication decreased the platelet count and caused new foci in the lungs. At the age of 27, respiratory failure occurred after another attempt at steroid cancelation, accompanied by subtotal lung damage observed on CT scans ( Figure 1A ). Despite antibiotic and antifungal (amphotericin) therapy, no improvement was observed. Thoracoscopic lung biopsy revealed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia. Optimal response was observed on high-steroid doses ( Figure 1B ) with slow de-escalation to low-dose regimen. However, as before, steroid tapering resulted in the recurrence of thrombocytopenia and lung lesions.
By the age of 30, the patient developed steroid hormone dependence with clinical and laboratory manifestations and also presented with Cushing's syndrome as an adverse effect. Moreover, CMV infection (4,000 copies/mL of CMV in bronchoalveolar lavage) was detected.
For further patient diagnosis, target panel sequencing of IEI-associated genes was performed. The sequencing detected heterozygous deletion of exons 1 and 2 in the PTPN2 gene. This variant has never been previously described in the literature. MLPA analysis confirmed the mutation; the examination of generally healthy parents showed its de-novo status. The literature suggests that the PTPN2 product inhibits the JAK-STAT pathway. Phosphorylation assays of STAT1 and STAT3 demonstrated hyperphosphorylation in patients with heterozygous mutations in PTPN2. In our case, the STAT1 phosphorylation assay also demonstrated hyperactivation of the STAT1 pathway ( Figure 2 ).
Considering the genetic results and the adverse side effects of steroid therapy, the immunosuppressive treatment was adjusted: the JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib was initiated at a dose of 15 mg per day. The dose was escalated to the optimal one according to the label:30 mg per day:after a month. Finally, the steroids were completely canceled after 3 months ( Figures 3A, B ).
The therapy was well-tolerated. Due to the development of mild CMV viremia (1,100 copies/mL) during the ruxolitinib therapy, valganciclovir was started at a 5-month period after JAK inhibitor initiation. In the 2-month treatment, no copy of CMV was detected and valganciclovir was continued in a prophylactic dose until 16 months of checkpoint when the therapy was completely canceled. Throughout this period, no virus was detected in the blood. The last control of CMV viremia was 6 months after valganciclovir cancellation and it still was negative. The patient had no signs of organ damage and no other herpes virus infection has been reported since JAK inhibitor initiation.
At the 3-month checkpoint, the patient had stable blood counts with a tendency toward an increase in platelets. A positive response was observed with CT scan visualization. After 9 months (6 months of monotherapy with ruxolitinib 30 mg per day), stable blood counts and decreased lymphadenopathy were observed. The patient gained 7 kg; all the foci previously presented on the CT scan vanished and no new foci appeared. Pneumatization in the basal sections of the lungs was improved and reticular changes became less prominent ( Figure 3C ). At the 16-month checkpoint, all the symptoms were still under control ( Figure 3D ). It is worth noting that the patient was still lymphopenic; therefore, he continued to receive prophylactic co-trimoxazole along with IVIG replacement therapy ( Table 1 ). Nevertheless, evaluation of STAT1 phosphorylation a year after JAK inhibitor initiation showed results comparable with protein phosphorylation in a conditionally healthy person ( Figure 2 ). In addition, the patient's social adaptation has benefited from the treatment: he has noted an improvement in his general wellbeing and has adopted a more positive outlook on his future. According to the SF-36 Health Survey conducted before and 16 months after ruxolitinib initiation, the patient's physical health score increased from 41.6 to 53.4 and his mental health score increased from 19.6 to 28.6 correspondingly. The numbers reflect the improvement of the patient's quality of life.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old Caucasian male with lifelong immune dysregulation, common variable immunodeficiency, and steroid-dependent cryptogenic organizing pneumonia and thrombocytopenia presented at age 30 with exogenous Cushing's syndrome and opportunistic pulmonary infection.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: With symptom onset at age 1.5 years (generalized lymphadenopathy), the patient developed autoimmune hemolytic anemia at age 16 (responsive to IVIG and steroids), followed upon steroid withdrawal by pneumonia, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, and immune thrombocytopenia (platelets 38 x 10^9/L). Diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) due to persistent lymphopenia and hypogammaglobulinemia, he received IVIG replacement, antimicrobials, and steroids (azathioprine caused agranulocytosis). At age 27, steroid tapering precipitated respiratory failure with subtotal lung involvement on CT; thoracoscopic lung biopsy showed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP), which responded only to high-dose steroids with recurrent thrombocytopenia and lung infiltrates on every taper attempt. By age 30, he developed severe steroid dependence and iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome.
subjective.past_medical_history: Inborn error of immunity / common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), autoimmune hemolytic anemia (age 16), chronic steroid-dependent immune thrombocytopenia, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (biopsy-proven at age 27), generalized reactive lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, history of azathioprine-induced agranulocytosis, and iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome. Parents healthy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent respiratory symptoms/dyspnea on steroid tapers, Cushingoid features, and later 7 kg weight gain and improved physical/mental wellbeing on ruxolitinib.

objective.physical_examination: Clinical features of exogenous Cushing's syndrome, generalized lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Persistent lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and steroid-dependent thrombocytopenia (initial nadir 38 x 10^9/L). Target genetic screening for SH2D1A (SN2D1A) and BIRC4 was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration and lymph node biopsy excluded hematologic malignancy and showed reactive lymphadenopathy. Serial chest CTs showed subtotal bilateral lung damage at age 27 (biopsy-proven cryptogenic organizing pneumonia on thoracoscopic lung biopsy) that resolved completely after 9-16 months of ruxolitinib. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) at age 30 detected active CMV infection (4,000 copies/mL), and blood PCR 5 months into ruxolitinib therapy detected mild CMV viremia (1,100 copies/mL). Targeted IEI gene panel sequencing and MLPA identified a novel de novo heterozygous deletion of exons 1 and 2 in the PTPN2 gene, with functional flow cytometry confirming hyperphosphorylation/hyperactivation of the STAT1 pathway.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with a novel de novo heterozygous PTPN2 exon 1-2 deletion causing STAT1 hyperactivation, immune dysregulation (CVID phenotype, autoimmune cytopenias, lymphadenopathy, and steroid-dependent cryptogenic organizing pneumonia), and opportunistic cytomegalovirus (CMV) pulmonary infection (BAL CMV load 4,000 copies/mL at age 30) and subsequent mild CMV viremia (blood CMV load 1,100 copies/mL during JAK inhibitor therapy). Initiated targeted JAK1/2 inhibition with oral ruxolitinib (15 mg/day escalated after 1 month to 30 mg/day), allowing complete discontinuation of systemic corticosteroids after 3 months. Mild CMV viremia at month 5 of ruxolitinib was cleared within 2 months using oral valganciclovir, which was continued prophylactically until month 16 and then stopped without viral recurrence 6 months later. At 9- and 16-month follow-ups on ruxolitinib plus prophylactic co-trimoxazole and IVIG, STAT1 phosphorylation normalized, platelets stabilized, pulmonary CT lesions completely vanished, and SF-36 quality-of-life scores improved.
